## Learning goals

You will compare a regression on the treatment with the same regression plus covariates. The file is again the social-pressure experiment, now as in QSS 4.4.1. The mailing was randomized, so the Neighbors coefficient is already a comparison created by design. Adding year of birth, household size, and whether the household voted in the 2004 primary should not move that coefficient much. That stability is what randomization buys. It is not a demonstration that "controlling for a few variables" repairs an observational study.

## 1. Two fits

Control is the reference category.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
social <- read_csv("data/social.csv") %>%
  mutate(messages = factor(
    messages,
    levels = c("Control", "Civic Duty", "Hawthorne", "Neighbors")
  ))
m1 <- lm(primary2006 ~ messages, data = social)
m2 <- lm(
  primary2006 ~ messages + yearofbirth + hhsize + primary2004,
  data = social
)
coef(m1)["messagesNeighbors"]
coef(m2)["messagesNeighbors"]
```

The Neighbors coefficient is about 0.081 without the covariates and about 0.080 with them. Both say: assigned the Neighbors mailing, turnout is about 8 percentage points higher than under Control, holding the other terms in that model fixed.

`primary2004` is a strong predictor of 2006 turnout. It is not a confounder here, because the mailing was assigned at random. Adding it changes precision more than it changes the point estimate. In an observational study the same move can change the estimate a lot, and only for the confounders you actually measured. A control that sits on the path from the treatment to the outcome can make the estimate worse. "We controlled for everything" is not a design.
